analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal leases for coal, oil, and gas on public lands and offshore waters.
analysis.headline: The Keep It in the Ground Act of 2017 was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or markup before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced by Sen. Jeff Merkley with 7 Democratic cosponsors, would have stopped the federal government from selling new leases for coal, oil, and natural gas on public lands and in offshore waters, including the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific oceans and the Gulf of Mexico. It also would have terminated most existing nonproducing federal leases, buying them back. The bill would have used federal land policy to shrink the fossil fuel supply, aimed at avoiding the most dangerous impacts of climate change. It was read twice and sent to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee — chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski — took no action on it for the rest of the two-year Congress. It never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the general public through reduced future fossil fuel extraction on federal lands and waters — the largest source of US federal emissions — and lower long-term climate-related costs. Communities near federal coal and offshore drilling areas would face fewer new extraction projects. Renewable energy companies would gain market share as a competing fossil supply channel was closed. The bill also contained carve-outs: leases could be renewed or extended to avoid breaching existing contracts, and exceptions were allowed for imminent national security threats.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, via less federal-land fossil extraction

how_it_helps.text: The bill declared it US policy to keep fossil fuels under federal lands and waters in the ground to avoid the most dangerous impacts of climate change, and prohibited new federal leases for coal, oil, oil shale, tar sands, and natural gas onshore.
It stopped new offshore oil and gas leasing in the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific oceans, the Gulf of Mexico, and all other Outer Continental Shelf areas.

It terminated existing nonproducing federal leases for fossil fuels, with buy-back payment to leaseholders, while allowing renewal or extension of a nonproducing lease if ending it would cause a material breach of an existing contract.
It allowed exceptions if the Energy Secretary determined there was an imminent national security threat that would be significantly reduced by granting one.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on fossil fuel companies that hold or seek federal leases — the federal onshore and offshore program is a major source of US oil, gas, and coal — and on their workers and the Gulf Coast, Alaska, and coal-region communities tied to that activity. Taxpayers would fund the buy-back of terminated nonproducing leases, and federal royalty revenue (shared with states) would decline over time as leases wound down. Consumers could face somewhat higher energy prices as the federal supply channel closed, though the bill does not touch production from existing producing leases, private land, or imports, so the effect on prices would likely be gradual. The long-run offset is avoided climate damage, which the bill itself cites as the benefit to "the people of the United States."
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel companies, leaseholders, and energy-region workers

drawbacks.text: The bill restricted only federal lands and waters; fossil fuel production could shift to private and state lands, other countries, or existing producing federal leases, which limits how much total emissions would actually fall and could raise energy costs for consumers without a proportional climate benefit.

The federal fossil fuel leasing program generates royalty revenue for the Treasury and for states like Alaska, Wyoming, and the Gulf Coast states; winding it down, plus buying back terminated nonproducing leases, would impose real fiscal costs and hit jobs and tax bases in energy-producing regions.

The bill itself acknowledged contract exposure: it created exceptions allowing nonproducing leases to be renewed or extended where termination would cause a material breach of contract, an admission that canceling leases carried legal and financial risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's central benefit — cutting the largest single source of US federal emissions by closing the federal leasing channel — was real and large in principle, but its design blunted it: existing producing leases, private land, and imports were untouched, so much production could simply shift rather than stop, meaning a large share of the cost (lost royalties, leaseholder losses, regional jobs) could be paid without the full climate payoff. An honest assessment is that the bill was a strong statement of climate policy with meaningful but partly leakable supply-side effects; its actual climate impact depended on how much extraction genuinely stopped rather than moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was filed, and the committee never held a hearing or markup, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on March 28, 2017; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
Seven senators cosponsored the bill, all Democrats.
No further action appears in the record: the committee took no hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill received no floor action for the remainder of the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies and federal leaseholders benefited from the bill's death: the federal government continued selling and honoring coal, oil, and gas leases on public lands and offshore waters exactly as before, with no new restrictions and no lease buy-backs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies with federal leases

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 28, 2017, sending it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it stayed in committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters (the sponsor and 7 cosponsors) were Democrats and no Republicans signed on; no vote was ever held, so the bill's fate was decided by the Republican-controlled committee, not by a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have barred new offshore and onshore federal leases, ending the industry's access to a major supply channel on public lands and waters. Its interest in killing the bill ran against the bill's climate benefits for the public.
New federal coal leases would have stopped and terminated nonproducing leases could not be reinstated, cutting off future federal coal supply. Federal coal is a major share of US coal production.

industries.industry: Federal fossil fuel leaseholders (incl. holders of nonproducing leases)
industries.note: Nonproducing leases would have been terminated with buy-back payment — a financial loss compensated in cash; the contract-breach renewal exception softened the hit for some leaseholders.
Closing the federal fossil fuel leasing channel would slow the growth of competing fossil supply, supporting demand for renewables; the bill contained no direct subsidies for the industry.
